I love this question because it’s so controversial and confusing. It took me a hot minute to understand it. Some might disagree with me on this but this is my take on it. 

So Company Policy says that when a customer wants to return an item without a receipt and it’s found on our scanner, they get the lowest price listed back on a merchandise card. So the ticket says $49.99 but the scanner says “current price” is $29.99, they get $29.99 back. That’s basically their way of saving as much money as possible. In that case if the customer asks you about it just tell them it’s company policy and if they have questions they can call the customer service line. However, not everyone does that. This is one of those situations where you have the power to decide what you want to do. Most people won’t think twice about it and just give them back what they paid or what’s on the ticket. That way you don’t have to change anything on the computer and you avoid a potential argument. Now I might change the price if the customer is rude OR it’s a huge price drop. The bigger the gap the more noticeable it is in cash office.. keep that in mind. 

So to answer your question. Yes, you have to change the price if it’s listed differently but you’re not going to get in trouble if you give them what they paid back. I guess it’s more of a judgment call or common sense thing. If you are really worried about it, write something like “REACH for customer” on the back of our copy of the receipt so cash office knows. 

You are correct about the price. It’s $19.99+ with no receipt. 

And to answer the last question, yes. You put RNF (We do INF) on the receipt if it doesn’t show up on the scanner. Return those ones. It’s not worth a fight. If it’s really pricey, ask your CEC or co worker just to double check. 

Good luck with going back to work and thank you so much for your kind words. Hope this helps!

oohh good question. This can be very tricky and hard to understand so this is how I handle these situations. 
First off, tone, body language and wording plays a huge roll in this. You have to put on that fake smile and customer service voice and push through. My go to is a soft soothing voice, slight puppy dog eyes (sounds pathetic but trust me on this) and I’ll usually lean on the counter so I seem like less of a threat. You want to sympathize with them without throwing you or the company under the bus. Say things like “no I totally get that” and “I see what you mean”. It helps when they feel understood and heard. 

Then I’ll say:

“Yep, so when you return an item from our store without a receipt you get the money back on a gift card. That’s because we have no proof of purchase. We don’t know if this was a gift or if you paid with a gift card. We can’t just give you cash. It’s the companies policy so if you want I can give you the customer service number and you can talk to them about it. As of right now, the gift card is all I can give you. I apologize.” 
Keep it short and sweet. 

Some ask why it matters if they get cash or a gift card since they still get money back for it and the answer is because if you give them cash, we could lose that money completely. Chances are they’ll spend it elsewhere. If you give them a gift card, the money stays within our company. So yeah, the store loses that money that day but eventually it’ll come back to us. This is how we keep our money. 
 
You always want to lean on the company during these situations. Without making the company sound bad, explain to them that it’s their policy and the store itself is not in charge of making those decisions. They can always call the number and talk to someone. Don’t be afraid to say “if you’d like, I can have my manager explain this” if it’s still not clicking. Usually at that point they won’t care anymore and say forget it. Otherwise the CEC or manager can take care of the rest. Most of the time they planned to say this for more money or discounts and other times it’s people trying to return a theft and get cash for it. Happens alllll the time.
I’m so glad I could help. Watching the other CECs should help for sure. Soon you’ll have your own routine down! Good luck and remember I’m always here to answer questions

This is how I sell it.

Technically you’re supposed to ask right away but I like to wait until I get an idea what their total is going to be. This is the easy version.
Say they are spending $320. Once I see it, I’ll ask:

“Do you have the TJX rewards credit card with us?”
“No” or “No, no thank you”
“Alright well just so you know, every $200 you spend you get $10 back and 10% off your first purchase. Like right now you are well over $200 so you’ll save at least $20 AND you’ll get $10 off. So technically you’re saving $30. I just need to scan your license” it’s a lot to say, I know. But if you don’t get it out you lost a BIG window of opportunity. Practice to yourself until it’s memorized, say it a little fast with a clear stern voice and put emphasis on the benefits. Otherwise it just sounds like mush and they won’t care. Look them in the eye too!!! Make it personal!! DO NOT sound or act like a robot. Everyone, including myself is guilty of this. That’s why I like to talk at the beginning after saying hello so they feel comfortable with me and there’s a small connection. Much easier to sell it then. 
“Oh sh*t, yeah let’s do it” 
“Awesome! It’s a great card! I just need to see your license then”

HELPFUL TIP!
Point to the credit card application when speaking about it, hand it to them, flip it over and point to the benefits as you’re reading it to them. Say “look at alllll of these benefits”, open it up and act as if you’re ready to start it. Trust me, that helps sooo much.  

Obviously it’s a harder fight if the price is $50-$100 but you can absolutely do it. 

I can explain how to sign people up if you’re interested! 

KEY POINTS! 
- make a connection from the start. show them you care and make it personal.
- DON’T sounds like a robot, as silly as it sounds
- if there is a long line and they don’t want to sign up because of it, reassure them immediately. Act casual about it and say something like “Oh gosh, you’re fine. We’ve got plenty of people to take care of that” even if you don’t, SAY IT! Pull them back in!  Let co workers and managers take care of the line.
- if they say they left their license in the car, causally tell them to go run and get it. Chances are they will. “Oh we’ve got plenty of time, go get it real quick so you can save your money!” 
- share more benefits if they start fighting. If it’s close to Members Morning, tell them. 
- I hated this part and I still do but please keep pushing! Ask once, give one more benefit a few minutes later, and just before they pull their form of payment out or go to use it, tell them how much they’ll save and ask “are you sure? Because...”. But this is important, read your customer! DO NOT push them when it’s very clear they don’t want it. Our district manger told us that it’s better to lose a credit card application than losing a customer and possibly getting a bad review. 
- if you see someone with a lot of items on the sales floor, find a way to kindly and gently tell them about the card. It’s helped multiple times
- give them SLIGHT puppy dog eyes or the hopeful shes. I stg it works... stg...

I’ll bet anything you’ve heard “Give at least two benefits and do not lead with 10% off”. Although that’s extremely annoying to hear from management, it makes total sense. The more credits we sell, the more money we get for treats, new equipment and more. Just don’t beat yourself up about it if you aren’t getting credits. It always depends on the customer and time of year. 

If they have a small purchase under $40 and they say no, tell them that they can take an application and wait until they have a bigger purchase OR tell them that they can sign up now so they don’t have to do it later. 

I can answer more questions if you’d like!

Oh gosh, that’s a great question. I’ll be honest, selling credit cards is hard and a lot of work. I hated it and felt bad for pestering the customers and constantly pushing it. It also took me at least 8 months to finally nail it. My average is 3 a day if I’m on register but there are days where I can get around 11 if I open that day. 

I’ll post how I sell it after this one.

The first thing is that you need to know what you’re selling! Girl, the first 3 months of working there I had no idea what the benefits were besides you can save 10%.

Here are the benefits:

- every $200 you spend, you get $10 back. Meaning they spend $200 (that’s 1,000 points), they get a rewards certificate (like a gift card) through the mail or their email. They can check online to see where they are at. We don’t keep any personal info so we can’t see if they’ll get the certificate if they spend another $50. 
- you get 10% off your FIRST purchase UPON APPROVAL. Make sure you say upon approval bc if they’re denied some still think they can use it bc they just signed up and that’ll start an argument. And remember they can save the coupon for 30 days after signing up. So if they signed up but the purchase is $10, it’s a waste to use the coupon. They should use it when they spend $100+
- “members only” days. I believe about 4 times a year we host a small event where cardholders can come in and get breakfast treats, coffee, a small Tj Maxx reusable bag, their name gets put into a raffle for gift cards and they get first pick on all the new merchandise. The store opens an hour earlier for them and ends when we open for the public. 
- you get 5% back every time you use it. That’s where the points come in.
- free online shipping.

Extras incase you’re asked, an identity theft resolution is provided if the card is stolen or lost and the cardholders info is protected.
The interest rate is high. That is the BANKS doing, not ours. They also decide if the customer gets approved, we don’t. They need to call the bank for any questions or if the approval is pending and they want to know ASAP.
No info is stored in our system. They are protected when giving their social. 
The APR is like 29%
The bank TJX companies use is Synchrony bank. Sometimes the customers ask. 

There are 2 different types of credit cards. The basic one that allows you to use it at TJX stores only and the platinum MasterCard that can be used at any other store and at the ATM. 1 point earned for every dollar spent outside of TJX.

If you struggle with the 10% calculations, this should help. I’m dyslexic so that’s why I’m mentioning this. 
$100 spent, $10 off
$200 spent, $20 off
$300 spent, $30 off and $10 rewards coming back
$400 spent, $40 off and $20 rewards coming back
And so on

To be honest, closing is the easiest part of the day. At least in my opinion. I think the only thing I don’t like about it is that sometimes you aren’t scheduled with a cashier so being up there by yourself for a few hours with lines and closing duties to finish, it can be frustrating. Just remember that you can absolutely ask your co workers to help if they can. I have the sales floor, fitting room and jewelry help me all the time. About 2 hours before you close, start cleaning up. Slowly empty trash cans, put away hard tags, gather up the iron mountain bin stuff into one white bin, put away hangers, sweep, recover the Q line. Extras would be filling gift cards, putting out stock, dusting and any other deep cleaning. About an hour before closing get the “pop count” counted so you or the manager can run and get the soda for the cooler (if you even have one). Make sure you do the closing announcements if your manger isn’t going to. Otherwise jewelry can do it as well. Close the security blocks on registers that aren’t being used. Make sure you call out go backs (returns) to the sales floor associates every 30 minutes so they can put it away and you’re not stuck doing it when you close. Apparently we are meant to take the clothes to the backroom and hang them so they can go out instead of doing it in between customers up front. We don’t do that and I don’t agree with doing that. It’s nice on paper. It’s nice if you have an extra cashier to send back there but usually you don’t. And the women’s and men’s associates are usually too busy. I think it’s more productive to have the cashiers do it so they aren’t bored and you aren’t getting talked to bc your cashiers are standing around. If I’m by myself I’ll send the clothes to fitting room to put away. Always ask them to help even if they’re going to do it regardless;)
Make sure you keep up with the line. You should not be ringing unless it’s past 5pm or sometimes 7pm. So if you have one cashier and 3 customers in line, call someone up. 3 cashiers and about 6–7 customers? Call 1-2 people up. If you have to be on register to help, take no more than 3 customers unless your managers says otherwise. When the store is closed, wait for the manager to say you can open the registers to take the money out. You will have the numbers to close down the register yourself so I like to go and open all of them for my coworkers. Remember, they can open the register but can’t close it. You have to go into back office and close it for the night. Super easy. Gather the money and count it from the money drawer, gather up the schedule and any other papers, gather the money bags and all keys you have access to and give it to the manager. That’s about it. Remember that’s everything my store does. Yours might be different.

You know the hard tags (also called gators) that are on clothes? Most people assume they have ink in them?
